title: Attest a proof run
goal: Every automated test's result at an exact commit is on record where nobody, including the CI run that produced it, can alter it afterwards.
notes: Decisions of 2026-10-29: Assuring owns run evidence and the release gate. The spec counts an obligation proved when a test record exists; Assuring shows that the test ran and passed at an exact commit. The evidence is a signed attestation kept by the CI provider with the commit as its subject, never a file that CI commits back, because a file for commit X can only land in commit X+1. The gate is a ratchet per obligation: a change may not take any obligation that was designed, built or proved at the base branch's head back to undone, while new obligations may arrive unproved so the spec can grow before its code; a release needs every obligation designed, built and proved with every automated proof passed at its commit. Outcome measures and audits stay outside Assuring. Today's prose specs retire one by one as the spec's records and the new evidence cover each one.

title: Gate a change
goal: A change merges only when it leaves STEGO at least as designed, built and proved as the branch it joins, and every proof passed at its commit.
notes: Decisions of 2026-10-29: Assuring owns run evidence and the release gate. The spec counts an obligation proved when a test record exists; Assuring shows that the test ran and passed at an exact commit. The evidence is a signed attestation kept by the CI provider with the commit as its subject, never a file that CI commits back, because a file for commit X can only land in commit X+1. Outcome measures and audits stay outside Assuring. Today's prose specs retire one by one as the spec's records and the new evidence cover each one. Decisions of 2026-10-31: the gate is built from the base head, never from the change, as the attest job runs none of the product's code. A removal, rename or merge of an obligation needs a retirement record, and the ratchet follows its successor. A branch rule at the provider requires a change to be up to date with main before it merges, so the change's tree is the tree that merges, the proof run proved that tree, and the comparison with main's head asks exactly whether merging lowers main. A pull request that edits a CI definition can never pass its own gate, because its proof run is change grade; it merges with a bypass after the owner's review, and the gate's output still shows the outcomes and the ratchet. A spec with errors cannot be measured: the gate gives no decision and names the errors.

title: Resolve a service's modules
goal: The service's module requirements hold the modules its generated code needs, resolved from exactly the source STEGO captured.
notes: Decisions of 2026-10-28: Building runs from generated source to a signed image; the platform side (CI, manifests, platform requirements) is Delivering. A rebuild from the same inputs gives the same bytes; every build runs offline from a recorded module cache; the archetype pins the Go SDK; images are built only from a reproducible build and its build record, on scratch; every image carries SPDX and CycloneDX SBOMs and a keyless signature whose identity is the platform's pinned build definition. Resolution writes the module requirements through the apply journal, so an interrupted resolution is completed or rolled back by Recover from an interrupted apply (ST-GEN-UC06), a use case of Generating, as R01 states.

title: Start a service declaration
goal: The author has a declaration that STEGO already accepts, and a place to put fills.
notes: A scaffold is valid as written, because each archetype supplies the smallest example content that checking accepts. An archetype that can be meaningfully empty, such as rest-crud, needs none. One that cannot, such as rpc-service, supplies a minimal proto file. An author who does not want that content asks for an empty scaffold, and STEGO then names every setting they must supply before checking will accept the declaration.

title: Learn what may be declared
goal: The agent knows every field, setting and slot it may write, before it writes any of them.
notes: Its step reads Supplying's query Report what may be declared (ST-SUP-QRY01), a deliberate deviation from keeping queries inside their domain: what may be declared is the registry, which Supplying owns, and the query reads it directly. A read changes no aggregate.

title: Check a declaration
goal: The author knows whether the declaration is acceptable, and the project is untouched either way.
notes: This use case relies on every invariant of the Declaration aggregate, which it applies rather than restates. Its own requirements say only how checking behaves: that it writes nothing, that it reports every fault, and that it happens once.

title: Repair a refused declaration
goal: The agent corrects the declaration from the refusal alone, with no person reading the message.
notes: This use case is why a refusal is data and not prose. STEGO's premise is that an agent writes the declaration, so the refusal is the agent's repair instruction.

title: Declare tenancy with its audit settings
goal: The author has a declaration whose tenancy and audit settings checking accepts, or knows which default it left without a reason.
notes: Tenancy and audit are on in every ga archetype. The author writes a setting only to leave a default, to name the claim path and key, or to mark an entity shared or system and a field pii or secret.

title: Declare authorization
goal: The author has a declaration that binds an authorization provider, names a schema kept in the service's own source, and states for each entity and slot what is checked and which relationships are written, all of which checking accepts against the compiled schema.
notes: Fills make authorization decisions and declare relationships, because which permission applies and which relationship a business action creates is essential complexity. The slot contract carries the tenant, the subject and an authz handle with Evaluate, Relate and Unrelate. A fill never gets a provider client.

title: Declare idempotent operations
goal: The author has a declaration that states which operations require an Idempotency-Key, how long a key is kept and what its fingerprint covers, and checking accepts it.
notes: The key is required on create. A replay returns the stored response byte for byte. The record commits with the write, in the transaction the adapter opens.

title: Declare a ledger
goal: The author has a declaration with an entity of kind ledger, its accounts and a collection over its transfers, and checking accepts it.
notes: The ledger follows the TigerBeetle model: a normal balance per account, one currency per ledger, a pending transfer that is immutable and is voided and pended again, and reversal as the only correction. There is no difference adjustment.

title: Declare a service's composition
goal: The author has a declaration that states the modes the one binary runs, the mixins it binds, its controllers and its invariants across stored instances, and checking accepts it.
notes: One binary runs the selected modes from a repeatable mode flag; all is the default and is allowed in production. Generation emits one Deployment per declared mode, an HPA on CPU by default and KEDA only when the platform requirements declare it. The ledger snapshot and check jobs run in controller mode.

title: Find every service built from a component
goal: A platform engineer names every service that was built from a given component digest.

title: Ship a component fix without a compiler release
goal: A fixed component reaches consumers without a new compiler version.
notes: Decision of 2026-10-27: one signed compiler holds every generator. A fix reaches consumers through per-component digests and a registry pin that moves apart from the compiler pin, not through a separately released generator.

title: Learn that a pinned component is superseded
goal: A service author finds out, while working, that a component the service pins has been superseded.
notes: The lifecycle records are read from the registry's current head, not from the pinned snapshot, so a consumer on an old snapshot still learns of a supersession.

title: Withdraw a component digest
goal: A component digest that must not be used any more stops being usable, and every affected service is named first.

title: Qualify a compiler release
goal: A release is qualified at an exact commit before anyone can install it.

title: Install a qualified compiler
goal: The operator installs a compiler whose identity and platform they can verify.

title: Measure the fleet
goal: The platform engineer reads each outcome measure of the fleet, computed from the swept records alone.

title: Publish a compiler release
goal: Every commit on main that passes the release gate becomes an installable release at that exact commit, immutable and never the latest, with no hand step.
notes: Decided 2026-10-31: the gate is the only arbiter of release quality, so a release follows a passed release decision automatically; a person publishing by hand would be a second gate the specification cannot check. Consumers pin full commits, so one release per commit changes nothing for them. The rules come from the retired prose policy on compiler installation (PR 18): one immutable tag per commit, four authenticated assets, never the latest, never a replaced tag, a burned tag needs a new merge commit.

title: State what a service needs from the platform
goal: The platform knows, from one typed file, everything a service needs from its environment, without reading its code.
notes: Decisions of 2026-10-29: STEGO owns everything derivable from the declaration, and the platform owns everything derivable from the environment. The Kubernetes base is a plain kustomize base; the platform's overlay supplies the image digest, namespace, replicas, PodDisruptionBudget and any change to the default resources. Every service writes its platform requirements with its secrets and configuration, backing services, network and cluster permissions. The environment check checks an environment file against them, by hand and in the CI of the platform's own project. The first providers are a hosted CI provider and Konflux (Tekton) for CI, and Argo CD for delivery. The hosted CI provider calls the platform's shared pipeline, pinned by commit; Konflux runs its standard pipeline from the generated Containerfile, and every STEGO check runs on both. Each provider names one trusted signer. The fleet stays a manual sweep: CI publishes no consumer manifest to an index.

title: Write a service's GitOps deployment
goal: A service's repo holds a plain Kubernetes base and, when the declaration asks for delivery, an Argo CD delivery object, each with only what the declaration derives, so that the platform's overlay supplies every environment value.
notes: Split from Deploy a service with GitOps (ST-DLV-UC05) on 2026-11-04: the Service author writes the base and the delivery object when the plan is applied, and the Operator deploys them. The delivery object is written by the policy ST-DLV-PO04, which hears Kubernetes base written, as Sign the built image (ST-BLD-PO02) hears Image built.

title: Add a service rule at a slot
goal: A service rule runs at the slot it belongs to, in code the agent or author wrote and tested, and no generated file is edited by hand.
notes: Decisions of 2026-10-28: a fill belongs to one project; the compiler refuses a bound fill with no tests, or one that is not qualified; qualified means recorded test evidence and a person's key signature of that evidence, both kept in the fill manifest; a fill imports only its slot contract, the standard library and the modules the declaration lists.

title: Qualify a fill
goal: A fill ships only after its tests passed against its contract and a person signed that evidence with their own key.
notes: Decisions of 2026-10-28: a fill belongs to one project; the compiler refuses a bound fill with no tests, or one that is not qualified; qualified means recorded test evidence and a person's key signature of that evidence, both kept in the fill manifest; a fill imports only its slot contract, the standard library and the modules the declaration lists. A signature proves that a holder of a listed key signed; only a key that needs a touch, such as a hardware key, proves that a person was present, and a team may require such keys in its SIGNERS file.

title: Find an existing fill for a slot
goal: An author or an agent reuses a fill that already implements a slot, instead of writing a second one.

title: Requalify a fill after a change
goal: A fill whose code, tests or contract changed ships again only after its tests pass and a person signs the new evidence.
notes: Decisions of 2026-10-28: a fill belongs to one project; the compiler refuses a bound fill with no tests, or one that is not qualified; qualified means recorded test evidence and a person's key signature of that evidence, both kept in the fill manifest; a fill imports only its slot contract, the standard library and the modules the declaration lists.

title: Record what a service was built from
goal: The service's repo holds a record of every input its generated code came from.
notes: Decision of 2026-10-27: the record extends the state file that STEGO keeps wherever it is used, and does not live in a second file.

title: Trust that a record matches its code
goal: A reader can trust that a service's record describes the generated code beside it.

title: Take a component fix into a service
goal: The service carries the fixed component, and the change is a diff a reviewer can read.
notes: Decision of 2026-10-27: a fix reaches a service as a pin bump and a new generation run, never as a hand edit, because a regenerated diff is auditable and a hand edit is not. Decision of 2026-10-28: Distributing owns the digest lifecycle, so its standing check runs before apply, and apply does not check standing itself. This step invokes Distributing's query, which goes outside the rule that a flow invokes its own domain's commands and queries.

title: Regenerate after a declaration change
goal: The service's generated code follows its changed declaration, and the change is a diff a reviewer can read.
notes: This is the main loop: an author or an agent changes the declaration, and a new run brings the code in line. Apply can run without a saved plan here, and then it plans in the same run.

title: Review a plan before anything changes
goal: The service author sees every file a run would change before any file changes, and apply then makes exactly those changes.
notes: Decision of 2026-10-28: a plan can be saved, under .stego/ as local working state that is not committed. Apply carries out a saved plan exactly, and can also run without one.

title: Recover from an interrupted apply
goal: After an apply stops part way, the generated files and the record agree again, and no hand-written change is lost.

title: Capture a frontend build as an input
goal: A service's frontend build becomes one checked input that generation reads, so generated code depends on no build folder or download.
notes: Decision of 2026-10-28: capturing browser assets is an input capture for Generating, like the proto files a generator reads.

title: See a service's architecture
goal: A service owner understands what their service is made of, how it is shaped and how a request moves through it, without reading code.
notes: Decisions of 2026-10-29: understanding is its own outcome (ST-BO09). Every apply writes the architecture view with the code, so the record covers it and a stale view is drift. It is one self-contained HTML file with no server and no network, and it shows structure, data model, request flows and platform edges.

title: Review how a change reshapes a service
goal: A reviewer sees how a declaration change or a component fix changes the shape of a service, and can trust that the view is current.
notes: Decisions of 2026-10-29: understanding is its own outcome (ST-BO09). Every apply writes the architecture view with the code, so the record covers it and a stale view is drift. It is one self-contained HTML file with no server and no network, and it shows structure, data model, request flows and platform edges.

title: Move a service to a new declaration version
goal: A service crosses a breaking compiler release within the window the registry's advisories give, and the fixer does the mechanical part of the rewrite.
notes: Decision of 2026-10-30: a declaration states its declaration version, and the registry declares the versions it accepts. A breaking compiler release supersedes the old version through the registry's advisories, with a fail date, which Distributing records. The fixer rewrites a declaration to the next version where it can and names what it cannot, as cargo fix and go fix do. The first step invokes Declaring's query List the faults of a declaration, outside the rule that a flow invokes its own domain's commands and queries, as ST-GEN-UC03 already does with Distributing's query.

title: Move a service to a promoted component
goal: A service that built from its team's local component builds from the same component in the common registry, after the platform team accepted it, and its generated code does not change.
notes: Split from Contribute a component upstream (ST-SUP-UC06) on 2026-11-04: the contribution ends when the common registry holds the component, and each service then moves its own pin, at a time of its author's choice.

title: Start a change to a table with rows
goal: The service author changes the stored shape of an entity whose table has rows, and the next release runs on the new shape while the release that runs now keeps running beside it, so that a rolling deploy loses no row and no write.
notes: The first of two releases of a schema change: this release adds (expand), the backfill moves the rows (ST-GEN-UC13), and the next release removes (ST-GEN-UC15). A rolling deploy runs one extra replica with no replica unavailable (ST-SUP-RC16-OC14), so both releases run at the same time. Owner decision of 2026-11-06 (Q5): a storage rename does not rename the API field; an API rename is a separate breaking change and is not in this design.

title: Backfill a changed column under the controller lease
goal: The operator deploys a release with a schema change at expand, and one controller replica moves every row to the new shape in short fenced batches, so that the next release can contract with no long lock and no two replicas write one row.
notes: The backfill follows the pattern of the ledger jobs (ST-SUP-RP08-LC08) and the audit anchor (ST-SUP-RP05-LC09): controller mode, a lease with a fencing token (ST-SUP-RP09, ST-STD-TXN-R15), and a checkpoint. A backfill in the migration job was rejected: one long transaction holds locks, and it has no lease. Its progress goes through the probe runtime (ST-SUP-RP12) as built-in observations. A rename, retype and require copy or convert values; a unique counts duplicate groups and changes no row.

title: Refuse a change that breaks the running version
goal: The service author learns, before a merge, whether a declaration change can run beside the version that runs now on a database that has rows, so that no release breaks the running service or loses its data.
notes: Owner decision of 2026-11-06 (Q2): STEGO cannot see production, so the version that runs now is the declaration at the change gate's base ref; the gate is built from base. A release skipped in production is the operator's risk, and the documentation says so. The change gate runs stego compat on each pull request; a fault fails the gate.

title: Finish a change to a table with rows
goal: The service author removes what only the old release needed, the old column and the trigger, after every row has its new value, so that the schema carries no debt and the next change starts clean.
notes: The second release of a schema change, one release after the expand (ST-GEN-INV33). The release before the contract step keeps running while the contract migration runs; the release before the expand step can no longer start (ST-SUP-RC01-OC11). Owner decision of 2026-11-06 (Q1): the finished change stays in the declaration, and only a declaration version bump (ST-GEN-UC10) may fold finished changes into a new baseline.

title: Write a component
goal: The platform engineer adds a part that every service can build from, and makes each accidental decision once.
notes: The ports and the slots a component names exist before it is added: a port is defined by Define a port (ST-SUP-UC07) and a slot by Declare a slot (ST-SUP-UC08), each a use case of its own, so adding a component changes the registry alone.

title: Compose a registry for a team
goal: A team may add parts of its own without weakening the parts everyone shares.

title: Curate an archetype
goal: A service author selects one archetype and gets a shape that works, with every port answered.

title: Introduce an experimental component
goal: A team may run ahead of the platform team, visibly and for a stated time, without reaching a golden path.
notes: The acceptance by name belongs to the Declaring domain: a declaration accepts an experimental component, and checking a declaration refuses one it does not accept. This use case only makes the component reachable on purpose. The experiment provides a port name of its own, which no ga component provides; that port is defined first by Define a port (ST-SUP-UC07), and graduation lets the component take over the real port name.

title: Graduate a component
goal: An experiment becomes a part everyone can rely on, once it meets the quality bar, and nobody is surprised by the change.
notes: Which services use a component is recorded by the Distributing domain. Supplying holds it in a read model of its own, which that domain's published events must feed. A missed sunset fails checking in the Declaring domain, because an acceptance there cannot outlive the component.

title: Contribute a component upstream
goal: A team that solved a shared problem in its local registry gives the solution to every team, and the common registry trusts it only after the platform team's review and the quality bar.
notes: Decision of 2026-10-28: STEGO is a flywheel; consumer teams find accidental complexity and contribute components upstream (ST-BO02).

title: Define a port
goal: A port exists with its contract, the meaning of each of its fields and its conformance tests, so every provider of the port is interchangeable.
notes: Decision of 2026-10-30: a port owns a conformance test suite, and every provider must pass it before it graduates to ga. A change to a port's meaning is a new port name, never an edit in place. A conformance pass is recorded as quality evidence of the kind port conformance.

title: Declare a slot
goal: A component offers a typed extension point whose contract can evolve without breaking the fills that bind to it.
notes: Decision of 2026-10-30: the breaking rule for a slot contract is Buf's FILE rule set. Declare a slot and Release a component version refuse a contract change that fails FILE unless the slot takes a new name. A slot that no generator invokes is refused by ST-SUP-INV06, and the Extending domain refuses a binding to such a slot; this use case cites those rules and does not restate them.

title: Choose a provider for a port
goal: The platform engineer finds every component that provides or requires a port, and picks the one an archetype answers the port with by default.
notes: Two ga providers of one port are interchangeable, because each passed the port's conformance tests. A provider that means something else by a field fails the suite, stays below ga, and so cannot be chosen.

title: Curate a golden path with its default concerns
goal: The platform engineer curates a ga archetype that carries tenancy and audit-log by default, binds the mixins a service may add and the mixins they require, and retires the event-publisher alias, so a service author gets the transactional concerns without choosing them.
notes: Decision of 2026-10-31, The Transactional Service: tenancy and audit are defaults of every ga archetype; authorization, idempotency and the ledger are bound on demand. Refusals are reported in this order: a missing default concern, an opt-out without a reason, a mixin without the mixin it requires, a default concern that is not ga.

title: Provide a port from the runtime library
goal: The platform engineer writes a component whose provider of a port lives in the runtime library, so the component emits only what varies with the declaration and the provider passes the port's conformance suite once for every service.
notes: Decision of 2026-10-31: code that is the same for every service lives in the runtime library, and a component emits only what the declaration changes. The SpiceDB provider of authz-decision is the first case. Refusals are reported in this order: a static file, a provider at an unpinned version, a missing conformance pass.

title: Retire a component
goal: An experiment that will not graduate goes before its sunset, and every service that uses it is told first, so no golden path and no service keeps it by surprise.
notes: Which services use a component is recorded by the Distributing domain. Supplying holds it in a read model of its own, which that domain's published events must feed. A missed sunset fails checking in the Declaring domain, because an acceptance there cannot outlive the component. Split from Graduate a component (ST-SUP-UC05) on 2026-11-04: the journeys ST-JR03 and ST-JR04 already have graduation and retirement as separate steps.
